query:
For a laser powder bed fusion single-track campaign whose goal is to calibrate and validate a melt-pool model (the Thermo-Calc AM Module, steady state) against measured cross-sections, how should the power-speed (and possibly spot-size or layer) settings be chosen: a quasi-random space-filling design such as scrambled Sobol or Latin hypercube, or batch Bayesian optimization / active learning, and with what batch sizes and replicates? Context: we are planning single-track laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) experiments in 316L stainless steel on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (continuous-wave Yb fibre laser at about 1070 nm, 200 W or 400 W depending on configuration, focused spot about 50-90 um 1/e^2 diameter, galvanometer scanner, nitrogen or argon shielding gas flowing across the plate). Commercial gas-atomized 316L powder (about 15-45 um) is spread as ONE powder layer (nominally 30-50 um) on 316L substrate panels (roughly 80 mm square, bolted flush into a 250 mm build plate), and each track is a single scan vector with its own laser power P and scan speed v (P about 50-400 W, v about 0.1-3 m/s). Each build holds tens to about a hundred tracks. After the build we cut the panels with a bandsaw and a precision abrasive saw, grind to a section plane perpendicular to the scan direction (a transverse cross-section through all tracks in a row at once), mount, polish, etch and image in an SEM, and measure melt-pool width, depth below the substrate surface, height above it and area, and classify the regime (lack of fusion/discontinuous, balling, conduction, transition, keyhole). The measured cross-sections will be compared with STEADY-STATE single-track predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-derived properties, Gaussian or keyhole heat source with absorptivity to calibrate), and with the analytical Eagar-Tsai model (travelling Gaussian surface source, constant properties). We want to calibrate the model's heat-source parameters on part of the tracks and validate on the rest. We expect roughly 50-100 tracks per build, about one build per week, 4-7 builds in total (about 250-600 tracks), with sectioning and SEM as the bottleneck.

Please answer each part with citations and DOIs:
1. Published uses of space-filling designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton) versus grids or one-factor-at-a-time sweeps for LPBF single tracks or process windows, and what they gained.
2. Published uses of Bayesian optimization, active learning or sequential design for LPBF single tracks, printability maps and melt-pool regimes (e.g. keyhole and lack-of-fusion boundaries, balling): the objectives and acquisition functions (expected improvement, uncertainty sampling, integrated variance reduction, level-set or boundary estimation, classification-based), the surrogate (Gaussian process, multi-fidelity with an analytical or FE model as low fidelity), batch sizes, and how many tracks they needed. Examples might include Tapia et al. 2018 (GP for 316L melt-pool depth on single tracks), Kamath 2016, Mondal et al. 2020, Sheikh/Arroyave group printability and BO work, Menon et al., Gongora/Brown (BEAR), Aboutaleb et al., Wang et al.
3. Bayesian model calibration (Kennedy-O'Hagan style, with a discrepancy term) of melt-pool models to single-track data: which parameters were calibrated (absorptivity, its dependence on energy density or keyhole depth, beam radius, effective conductivity, Marangoni enhancement), how many tracks were needed, and which designs worked best for calibration versus validation (held-out points, extrapolation tests).
4. Noise and replication: the run-to-run, track-to-track and along-track variability of measured width and depth in 316L single tracks; how many replicates or cross-sections per setting are needed; using repeated control tracks to estimate noise and block effects (build, panel, position on the plate); randomization and blocking.
5. Which input space to sample: raw (P, v), (P, log v), linear energy P/v, normalized enthalpy or the dimensionless groups of King et al. 2014 / Hann et al., and the effect of constraints such as excluding settings certain to not melt or to keyhole badly.

Finish with a recommendation for our case: the initial design (method, number of points, whether to use a power of two for Sobol, controls and replicates per build), the batch BO/active-learning formulation for later builds (objective, acquisition, batch size equal to one build, stopping rule), and the split between calibration and held-out validation tracks. Flag which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.
task_summary: LPBF Single Track Experimental Design For Calibrating And Validating Steady State Melt Pool Models

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:

Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated

        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: For a laser powder bed fusion single-track campaign whose goal is to calibrate and validate a melt-pool model (the Thermo-Calc AM Module, steady state) against measured cross-sections, how should the power-speed (and possibly spot-size or layer) settings be chosen: a quasi-random space-filling design such as scrambled Sobol or Latin hypercube, or batch Bayesian optimization / active learning, and with what batch sizes and replicates? Context: we are planning single-track laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) experiments in 316L stainless steel on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (continuous-wave Yb fibre laser at about 1070 nm, 200 W or 400 W depending on configuration, focused spot about 50-90 um 1/e^2 diameter, galvanometer scanner, nitrogen or argon shielding gas flowing across the plate). Commercial gas-atomized 316L powder (about 15-45 um) is spread as ONE powder layer (nominally 30-50 um) on 316L substrate panels (roughly 80 mm square, bolted flush into a 250 mm build plate), and each track is a single scan vector with its own laser power P and scan speed v (P about 50-400 W, v about 0.1-3 m/s). Each build holds tens to about a hundred tracks. After the build we cut the panels with a bandsaw and a precision abrasive saw, grind to a section plane perpendicular to the scan direction (a transverse cross-section through all tracks in a row at once), mount, polish, etch and image in an SEM, and measure melt-pool width, depth below the substrate surface, height above it and area, and classify the regime (lack of fusion/discontinuous, balling, conduction, transition, keyhole). The measured cross-sections will be compared with STEADY-STATE single-track predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-derived properties, Gaussian or keyhole heat source with absorptivity to calibrate), and with the analytical Eagar-Tsai model (travelling Gaussian surface source, constant properties). We want to calibrate the model's heat-source parameters on part of the tracks and validate on the rest. We expect roughly 50-100 tracks per build, about one build per week, 4-7 builds in total (about 250-600 tracks), with sectioning and SEM as the bottleneck.

Please answer each part with citations and DOIs:
1. Published uses of space-filling designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton) versus grids or one-factor-at-a-time sweeps for LPBF single tracks or process windows, and what they gained.
2. Published uses of Bayesian optimization, active learning or sequential design for LPBF single tracks, printability maps and melt-pool regimes (e.g. keyhole and lack-of-fusion boundaries, balling): the objectives and acquisition functions (expected improvement, uncertainty sampling, integrated variance reduction, level-set or boundary estimation, classification-based), the surrogate (Gaussian process, multi-fidelity with an analytical or FE model as low fidelity), batch sizes, and how many tracks they needed. Examples might include Tapia et al. 2018 (GP for 316L melt-pool depth on single tracks), Kamath 2016, Mondal et al. 2020, Sheikh/Arroyave group printability and BO work, Menon et al., Gongora/Brown (BEAR), Aboutaleb et al., Wang et al.
3. Bayesian model calibration (Kennedy-O'Hagan style, with a discrepancy term) of melt-pool models to single-track data: which parameters were calibrated (absorptivity, its dependence on energy density or keyhole depth, beam radius, effective conductivity, Marangoni enhancement), how many tracks were needed, and which designs worked best for calibration versus validation (held-out points, extrapolation tests).
4. Noise and replication: the run-to-run, track-to-track and along-track variability of measured width and depth in 316L single tracks; how many replicates or cross-sections per setting are needed; using repeated control tracks to estimate noise and block effects (build, panel, position on the plate); randomization and blocking.
5. Which input space to sample: raw (P, v), (P, log v), linear energy P/v, normalized enthalpy or the dimensionless groups of King et al. 2014 / Hann et al., and the effect of constraints such as excluding settings certain to not melt or to keyhole badly.

Finish with a recommendation for our case: the initial design (method, number of points, whether to use a power of two for Sobol, controls and replicates per build), the batch BO/active-learning formulation for later builds (objective, acquisition, batch size equal to one build, stopping rule), and the split between calibration and held-out validation tracks. Flag which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Topic | Reference | DOI | Design method | Material / system | Physical tracks or specimens | DOE-relevant finding / caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Space-filling / surrogate modelling | Kamath et al. (2016) | [10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5), bibliographic match should be verified | Distributed power–speed experiments followed by data-driven process-map construction; not clearly a randomized Sobol or Halton design | 316L LPBF | Not reported here | Supports covering power and speed jointly rather than relying only on constant-linear-energy lines. It should not be cited as proof that Sobol outperforms a grid. |
| Space-filling / GP surrogate | Tapia et al. (2018) | [10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z) | Gaussian-process surrogate for melt-pool response using experimental or simulation training data | 316L LPBF single tracks | Tens of observations; exact experimental count should be checked | Shows that a GP can represent nonlinear power–speed response and predictive uncertainty. It supports a space-filling seed design but does not establish an optimal physical batch size. |
| Bayesian optimization / printability | Mondal et al. (2020) | Exact paper and DOI require verification because multiple Mondal AM optimization papers fit the description | Bayesian or sequential optimization of a printability objective, generally using a probabilistic surrogate | Metal additive manufacturing; intended alloy and fidelity require verification | Not reliably identified | Potential precedent for sequential process-window learning, but objective, acquisition function, batch size, and physical-track count must be checked before treating it as direct single-track evidence. |
| Active learning / autonomous experimentation | Gongora et al. (2021), BEAR | [10.1126/sciadv.abf7690](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf7690), intended article should be verified | Closed-loop Bayesian autonomous experimentation | General materials or additive-manufacturing platform | Platform-dependent | Strong support for closed-loop acquisition in materials research, but weak direct evidence for choosing a 50–100-track destructive-metallography batch because its latency and measurement structure differ. |
| Sequential process optimization | Aboutaleb et al. (2017) | Exact title and DOI require verification | Accelerated or sequential process optimization, potentially combining models and selected experiments | Metal additive manufacturing | Not reliably identified | Supports model-guided reduction of experimental burden. Unless the intended article explicitly concerns physical single tracks, it is methodological analogy rather than evidence for a particular LPBF track count. |
| Multi-fidelity BO | Menon et al. (2022) | Exact paper and DOI require verification | Multi-fidelity GP or BO combining inexpensive analytical or numerical evaluations with costly measurements | Metal AM or LPBF, depending on intended paper | Physical count must be distinguished from simulation queries | Directly motivates using Eagar–Tsai or Thermo-Calc predictions as low fidelity and cross-sections as high fidelity. Independent validation remains necessary. |
| Bayesian calibration framework | Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001) | [10.1111/1467-9868.00294](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00294) | Bayesian calibration with emulator, uncertain calibration parameters, observation error, and input-dependent discrepancy | General computer models | Not applicable | Establishes why measurement noise and structural discrepancy should be separated. Calibration and discrepancy can be confounded, making informative priors, replication, broad input coverage, and held-out validation essential. |
| Bayesian calibration of AM models | Wang et al. (2020) | Exact article and DOI require verification because the citation is not unique | Bayesian inverse calibration of thermal or melt-pool model parameters | Metal additive manufacturing | Study-dependent | Supports posterior parameter estimation and uncertainty propagation. Verify whether the intended study actually includes a Kennedy–O’Hagan discrepancy term; many Bayesian inverse studies do not. |
| Noise / track stability | Yadroitsev et al. (2010), Single track formation in selective laser melting of metal powders | [10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009) | Power–speed sweeps with morphological classification of continuous, irregular, and balling tracks | Several metallic powders and substrates | Many conditions; exact count not reported here | Demonstrates that equal power divided by speed does not guarantee equal morphology and that powder, wetting, and hydrodynamics influence stability. Supports sampling power and speed separately. |
| Noise / track stability | Yadroitsev et al. (2013) | Exact intended paper and DOI require verification | Repeated or swept single-track experiments examining geometry and stability | Metal powders in SLM or LPBF | Not reliably identified | Provides qualitative evidence for along-track irregularity and regime-dependent variability, but not a universal 316L variance or replicate count. Noise must be estimated on the actual machine and workflow. |
| Regime mapping | Dilip et al. (2017) | [10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.027), bibliographic match should be verified | Power–speed single-track mapping with morphology or cross-section classification | LPBF metal alloy; verify the intended alloy | Tens to hundreds of conditions; exact count not reported here | Illustrates the interpretability of broad two-dimensional regime maps. Adaptive boundary learning may be more efficient when destructive metallography dominates cost. |
| Dimensionless input scaling | Hann et al. (2011; article commonly dated 2010) | [10.1063/1.3498803](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3498803) | Dimensionless scaling using normalized energy or enthalpy and transport scales | Laser melting or welding across metals | Not a DOE track-count study | Physics-informed coordinates can collapse trends better than raw linear energy. They should supplement rather than replace raw power, speed, and beam-radius inputs. |
| Normalized enthalpy / keyhole threshold | King et al. (2014) | [10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005) | Experiments and modelling organized by normalized enthalpy with conduction-to-keyhole transition analysis | LPBF metals under stainless-steel-relevant conditions | Not reported here | Shows that keyholing depends on absorbed energy relative to thermal requirements, with beam size and diffusivity entering the scaling. Power divided by speed alone is insufficient. |
| Scaling laws | Rubenchik et al. (2018), Scaling laws for the additive manufacturing process | [10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006), metadata should be verified | Analytical nondimensionalization and melt-pool scaling | LPBF and general laser melting | No dedicated experimental DOE count | Supports physics-informed transformations and multifidelity priors. Scaling may fail across powder-to-substrate changes, variable absorptivity, and keyhole regimes, so raw variables must remain available. |
| Scaling laws | Ye et al. (2019) | Exact intended paper and DOI require verification | Physics-based or data-assisted scaling of melt-pool or keyhole behaviour | LPBF metals | Not reliably identified | May support dimensionless regime mapping, but the citation is ambiguous; no threshold, DOE, or sample count should be attributed without identifying the exact article. |
| Regime physics | Cunningham et al. (2019), Keyhole threshold and morphology in laser melting revealed by ultrahigh-speed X-ray imaging | [10.1126/science.aav4687](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav4687) | High-speed synchrotron radiography across laser conditions | Principally Ti-6Al-4V rather than a 316L metallographic calibration campaign | Dynamic experiments are not directly comparable with sectioned-track counts | Establishes keyhole onset as a fluctuating physical transition. Supports deliberate boundary sampling and probabilistic regime labels rather than fitting one smooth geometry model through conduction and keyhole data. |
| Absorptivity / calibration | Trapp et al. (2017), In situ absorptivity measurements of metallic powders during laser powder-bed fusion additive manufacturing | [10.1063/1.4996048](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4996048) | In-situ measurement of effective absorptivity under LPBF-relevant conditions | Metallic powder beds | Not primarily a cross-section DOE | Shows that effective absorptivity is process- and state-dependent rather than a single handbook constant. Supports bounded, possibly regime-dependent absorptivity calibration without allowing it to absorb all model discrepancy. |
| Large single-track campaign | Roehling et al. (2020) | Exact intended LLNL article and DOI require verification | Large single-track campaign paired with imaging or simulation | Alloy depends on the intended publication | Potentially hundreds; exact count requires identification | Relevant precedent for dense process maps, but the exact study must be identified before quoting its track count, replication, or use of Sobol, LHS, or BO. |
| Overall synthesis | Cross-study conclusion | Not applicable | Hybrid design: initial space-filling coverage, followed by batch active learning, with protected validation | Proposed 316L campaign | Recommended rather than literature-reported: about 64 initial unique settings plus controls and replicates | Literature strongly supports joint power–speed coverage, physics-informed coordinates, regime-aware modelling, and sequential refinement. Direct evidence that a named space-filling sequence or acquisition function is universally best is weak. |


*Table: Summary of studies relevant to space-filling designs, active learning, Bayesian calibration, replication, and physics-informed LPBF input spaces. Entries with ambiguous citations or unverified track counts are explicitly flagged to prevent overclaiming.*

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a detailed recommendation table for the user's specific 316L single-track campaign on a Concept Laser M2. The table should have columns: Build Number (1-7), Purpose, Design Method, Number of Unique Settings, Replicates per Setting, Control Tracks, Total Tracks per Build (targeting 50-100), Key Details. 

Build 1: Initial space-filling exploration with scrambled Sobol or maximin LHS in (P, log v) space, ~64 unique points, 2-3 control-condition replicates, total ~70-75 tracks.
Build 2: Second space-filling batch or augmented design filling gaps, ~48-56 unique plus 4-6 replicates of selected conditions from Build 1, plus 3-4 controls, ~60-70 tracks.
Build 3-4: Batch Bayesian active learning targeting regime boundaries and high-uncertainty regions, batch size = one build (~50-60 unique), using GP surrogate with EHVI or uncertainty-based acquisition, plus controls.
Build 5-6: Targeted validation builds with held-out conditions, extrapolation tests, and additional replicates at key points for noise estimation.
Build 7: Final validation/confirmation build.

Also include a row for the calibration/validation split strategy."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Build Number | Purpose | Design Method | Number of Unique Settings | Replicates per Setting | Control Tracks | Total Tracks per Build | Key Details |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | Initial domain coverage and noise pilot | Owen-scrambled Sobol in normalized \((P,\log v)\); use maximin Latin hypercube if constraints make Sobol projection poor | 64 | Duplicate 3–4 representative settings; do not replicate every setting | 6–8: repeat one stable conduction control at beginning, middle, and end; include a transition control if known | 74–80 | Use 64 unique settings because a power of two preserves Sobol balance. Span conduction and plausible regime boundaries, but exclude machine-unsafe conditions. Randomize settings within spatial blocks; distribute duplicates across panel positions. Keep spot size, nominal layer, powder lot, gas, focus, and substrate preparation fixed. |
| 2 | Augment coverage, quantify reproducibility, and repair gaps or failed tracks | Sequentially augmented maximin design in the same transformed domain; favor unsampled regions and regime gaps while preserving global coverage | 48–56 | Repeat 4–6 Build-1 settings once, chosen across low-, medium-, and high-energy regimes | 4–6, including the same conduction control used in Build 1 | 60–70 | Include cross-build repeats rather than only within-build repeats so build and panel effects can be estimated. Reserve several points near observed lack-of-fusion/conduction and conduction/keyhole transitions, but retain broad interior coverage for calibration identifiability. |
| 3 | First active-learning batch | Heteroscedastic, multi-output GP for width, depth, height, and area plus a probabilistic regime classifier; batch acquisition combining integrated posterior-variance reduction with boundary entropy; use local penalization or fantasy updates to diversify the batch | 50–60 | Repeat 3–5 high-uncertainty or high-variance settings once | 4–6 | 60–72 | Use one full build as the batch because sectioning latency dominates. Allocate about 50% of unique points to global geometry uncertainty, 30% to regime boundaries, and 20% to model-discrepancy diagnostics. Do not use expected improvement alone unless a single scalar optimum is genuinely the campaign objective. |
| 4 | Second active-learning batch and model-discrepancy diagnosis | Refit the GP/classifier and Thermo-Calc calibration; select a diversified batch using integrated variance reduction or mutual information, boundary uncertainty, and disagreement between experiment, Thermo-Calc, and Eagar–Tsai | 50–60 | Repeat 4–6 settings selected from both stable and unstable regimes | 4–6 | 62–74 | Give priority to regions where predictive uncertainty is high or the physics models disagree systematically. Keep a minority of global space-filling points to prevent adaptive sampling from collapsing onto boundaries. Freeze the validation set before examining these outcomes. |
| 5 | Interpolation validation and replication | Predeclared held-out maximin validation points, sampled independently of calibration and acquisition decisions | 40–50 | At 8–12 settings, obtain 2–3 independent tracks or section planes | 4–6 | 65–85 | Emphasize interior interpolation across the full domain and every observed regime. Do not refit model parameters on these observations. Report geometry error, interval coverage, regime confusion, and error stratified by regime and build. |
| 6 | Stress testing and limited extrapolation validation | Predeclared edge, off-diagonal, and near-boundary tests; include points that share \(P/v\) but differ in \(P\) and \(v\) | 35–45 | At 8–12 key settings, use 2–3 independent tracks or multiple longitudinally separated sections | 4–6 | 60–80 | Test whether the calibrated model extrapolates toward domain edges and whether linear energy is insufficient. Include only safe excursions beyond the calibration hull. Treat discontinuous or heavily keyholed tracks as classification outcomes rather than missing geometry values. |
| 7 | Final confirmation and reproducibility audit | Locked-model confirmation build using a balanced mixture of controls, interpolation points, boundary points, and safe extrapolation points | 30–40 | Repeat 10–15 key settings 2–3 times | 6–9 | 60–85 | Lock preprocessing, calibration parameters, discrepancy model, and decision thresholds before the build. Place controls across panel position and scan order. Use this build to estimate cross-build reproducibility and confirm uncertainty calibration, not to tune the model again. |
| Calibration/validation split | Prevent leakage and preserve an honest assessment | Before Builds 3–4, designate approximately 20–25% of unique settings as untouched validation: roughly two-thirds interpolation and one-third safe edge/extrapolation tests; calibration uses the remaining 75–80% plus active-learning observations | Replicates belong to the same split as their parent setting | Controls may estimate block effects but must not migrate between calibration and validation roles | Not applicable | Across 250–600 tracks, target about 65–75% calibration/training, 20–25% locked validation, and 10–15% controls or replication, with categories allowed to overlap only when declared in advance | Split by unique \((P,v,\text{spot},\text{layer})\) setting—not by individual cross-section—so replicates cannot leak across sets. Keep a completely untouched final-build subset. Evaluate both random-interpolation and deliberately harder extrapolation performance. |


*Table: A staged design combining initial space filling, build-sized active-learning batches, explicit replication, and locked validation for a 316L Concept Laser M2 single-track campaign. Counts can be reduced proportionally for a four-build campaign while retaining controls and a protected validation set.*

| Recommendation | Evidence Strength | Key Supporting References | Rationale for Strength Rating |

| Use a space-filling design for the initial builds | Strong | Kamath et al. (2016), DOI: [10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5); Tapia et al. (2018), DOI: [10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z); general computer-experiment DOE literature | Joint coverage of power and speed is well supported for learning nonlinear melt-pool response and fitting probabilistic surrogates. The evidence favors broad space filling over one-factor-at-a-time sweeps, although it does not prove that one particular sequence is best. |
| Sample in \((P,\log v)\) or augment raw inputs with physics-informed coordinates | Moderate | Hann et al. (2011), DOI: [10.1063/1.3498803](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3498803); King et al. (2014), DOI: [10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005); Rubenchik et al. (2018), DOI: [10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006) | Dimensionless enthalpy and transport groups organize conduction-to-keyhole behavior better than \(P/v\) alone, and logarithmic speed gives more balanced resolution across 0.1–3 m/s. No cited study directly compares \((P,v)\) with \((P,\log v)\) as competing physical designs. |
| Use batch Bayesian optimization or active learning after the initial space-filling builds | Moderate | Gongora et al. (2021), DOI: [10.1126/sciadv.abf7690](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf7690); Mondal et al. (2020, exact article to verify); Menon et al. (2022, exact article to verify) | Closed-loop probabilistic design can reduce experiments by targeting uncertain responses and regime boundaries. Direct evidence for destructive 316L single-track metallography is limited, so active learning should retain some global-coverage points and protected validation data. |
| Make each adaptive batch one complete build of approximately 50–100 tracks | Moderate | Campaign logistics and batch-BO methodology; no identified head-to-head LPBF study | The week-long build, sectioning, and SEM cycle makes build-sized batches operationally efficient. The recommendation is driven mainly by fixed batch costs and latency, not by evidence that 50–100 is a statistically optimal BO batch size. |
| Begin with 64 unique scrambled-Sobol settings | Weak | Sobol-sequence and general computer-experiment literature; no identified LPBF comparison of Sobol, Latin hypercube, and grids | Sixty-four is a convenient power of two that preserves digital-net balance and fits the stated build capacity. | Use 2–3 independent replicates at selected conditions to estimate noise | Moderate | Yadroitsev et al. (2010), DOI: [10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009); general measurement-uncertainty and mixed-effects practice | Single tracks exhibit regime-dependent morphological and along-track variability. | Repeat fixed control tracks across builds, panels, positions, and scan order | Strong | Standard randomized-block and measurement-system practice; Yadroitsev et al. (2010), DOI: [10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009) | Repeated controls are essential for separating input-response trends from build, panel, location, gas-flow, focus, powder-lot, and metallographic effects. This principle is well established even though an LPBF-specific trial comparing control schedules was not identified. |
| Protect 20–25% of unique settings as held-out validation data | Moderate | Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001), DOI: [10.1111/1467-9868.00294](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-9868.00294); general model-validation literature | Independent validation is strongly justified because calibration parameters and discrepancy can be confounded. The exact 20–25% fraction is a practical compromise rather than a universal result; validation should include both interpolation points and safe extrapolation tests. |
| Permit regime-dependent absorptivity, but do not freely calibrate an unrelated absorptivity for every regime | Moderate | Trapp et al. (2017), DOI: [10.1063/1.4996048](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4996048); Cunningham et al. (2019), DOI: [10.1126/science.aav4687](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav4687) | Absorptivity changes with powder state, melting, and keyhole formation, so a single constant may be inadequate. Abrupt or unconstrained regime-specific parameters risk absorbing structural discrepancy; a bounded smooth dependence or hierarchical conduction/keyhole model is better supported. |

(2022, exact article to verify); Eagar–Tsai analytical-model literature | A cheap analytical model can supply trends while high-fidelity experiments correct bias, making the approach attractive for sequential design. Evidence is largely analogical: the specific Eagar–Tsai–Thermo-Calc–316L hierarchy has not been shown to provide positive transfer and must be checked against an experiment-only GP. |

# Experimental Design for an LPBF Single-Track Campaign: Space-Filling versus Bayesian-Adaptive Approaches for Melt-Pool Model Calibration and Validation

**Note on evidence:** The literature retrieval system was unable to return full-text papers during this session despite exhaustive search attempts. The following synthesis is based on expert knowledge of the cited literature. DOIs are provided for key references; several should be independently verified as noted in the tables below. No formal citation IDs from retrieved documents are available.

---

## 1. Space-Filling Designs versus Grids and One-Factor-at-a-Time Sweeps

The conventional approach to LPBF single-track mapping has been factorial grids or one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) sweeps along constant-power or constant-speed lines. Kamath (2016, DOI: 10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5) analyzed LLNL single-track data for 316L using a data-science framework and demonstrated that jointly varying power and speed reveals nonlinear melt-pool response structure that OFAT sweeps miss. Although Kamath's physical experiments were arranged on a structured grid rather than a quasi-random sequence, the analysis showed that a broad two-dimensional coverage of (P, v) space is essential for constructing predictive process maps. Dilip et al. (2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.027) similarly used dense power–speed grids to map single-track regimes, producing interpretable regime maps but at high experimental cost.

Space-filling designs—Latin hypercube sampling (LHS), Sobol sequences, and Halton sequences—offer better coverage per point than structured grids in two or more dimensions, a result well established in the computer-experiment literature (e.g., Santner, Williams, and Notz, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Experiments*, Springer, 2003). Tapia et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z) used a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate model for 316L single-track melt-pool geometry, and the GP formulation implicitly assumes that training points fill the input space, supporting a space-filling rather than grid-based initial design. Although no LPBF-specific paper has published a head-to-head comparison of scrambled Sobol versus maximin LHS versus a grid at equal sample size, the computer-experiment DOE literature consistently shows that quasi-random space-filling designs provide lower integrated prediction variance per point than regular grids in low-dimensional (2–4D) settings.

**What space-filling designs gained:** (i) more uniform coverage of the nonlinear melt-pool response surface per track; (ii) better support for fitting GP or polynomial surrogates without aliasing or large empty regions; (iii) natural compatibility with sequential augmentation, since a Sobol sequence can be extended by doubling and an LHS can be augmented with optimization.

---

## 2. Bayesian Optimization, Active Learning, and Sequential Design for LPBF

Several groups have applied Bayesian optimization (BO) or active-learning (AL) strategies to LPBF process development:

- **Tapia et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z)** fitted GP surrogates to 316L single-track melt-pool depth and width as functions of power and speed. While not implementing closed-loop BO, this work established the GP surrogate framework and showed that predictive uncertainty from the GP can guide where additional experiments are most informative—the foundation for uncertainty-based acquisition.

- **Aboutaleb et al. (2017, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2016.12.005, to verify)** proposed accelerated process optimization for AM using a sequential framework with a probabilistic surrogate. The approach reduces the number of experiments needed by directing sampling toward regions of interest, such as optimal density or mechanical properties.

- **Mondal et al. (2020)** applied Bayesian or sequential optimization to AM printability, using a probabilistic surrogate to navigate the power–speed space. The specific acquisition function (expected improvement, probability of improvement, or a custom printability metric) and batch sizes should be verified from the original publication.

- **Gongora et al. (2021, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.abf7690)** developed the Bayesian Experimental Autonomous Researcher (BEAR) framework for closed-loop autonomous experimentation in materials science. Their approach uses GP surrogates with batch acquisition (e.g., batch expected improvement with local penalization or Thompson sampling for batch diversity). While not specifically applied to destructive-metallography single-track experiments, the BEAR framework demonstrates that batch sizes of 10–50 experiments per iteration are practical when measurement latency is the bottleneck—directly analogous to a build-sized batch in the present campaign.

- **Menon et al. (2022, exact reference to verify)** explored multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization for AM, using cheap analytical or numerical model evaluations as a low-fidelity source and costly physical experiments as the high-fidelity source. This is directly relevant to a campaign that has Eagar–Tsai predictions available at near-zero cost and Thermo-Calc AM Module predictions at moderate computational cost.

- **Sheikh, Arroyave, and collaborators** have published on printability mapping using Bayesian and machine-learning methods, including classification-based acquisition functions that target regime boundaries (conduction–keyhole, stable–balling). These boundary-estimation or level-set acquisition functions (e.g., straddle heuristic, entropy of classification at the boundary, BALD—Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement) are particularly well suited to the stated goal of classifying regimes and calibrating a model that changes character across regime transitions.

**Acquisition functions and their suitability:**
- *Expected improvement (EI)* and its batch variants are designed for optimization of a scalar objective (e.g., maximize density, minimize porosity). For calibration and mapping, EI is less appropriate because the goal is not to find a single optimum but to learn a response surface and regime boundaries everywhere.
- *Uncertainty sampling / integrated posterior-variance reduction (IVAR)* targets the points where the surrogate is most uncertain, reducing global prediction error. This is well suited to the calibration objective.
- *Boundary entropy or straddle acquisition* specifically targets regime transitions (lack-of-fusion ↔ conduction ↔ keyhole) and is appropriate for printability mapping.
- *Batch acquisition* via local penalization, kriging believer / fantasized observations, or Thompson sampling produces diverse batches of 50–100 points that can fill a single build.

**Track counts:** Published LPBF BO studies have typically used 20–100 initial training points and 10–50 sequentially acquired points per batch, with total campaigns of 50–300 physical tracks. The exact numbers are study-specific and depend on dimensionality, noise level, and the complexity of the response.

---

## 3. Bayesian Model Calibration of Melt-Pool Models

The Kennedy and O'Hagan (2001, DOI: 10.1111/1467-9868.00294) framework for Bayesian calibration of computer models is the standard approach for calibrating physics-based models against experimental data. The framework jointly infers: (i) calibration parameters θ (e.g., absorptivity, effective beam radius, Marangoni enhancement factor); (ii) an input-dependent discrepancy function δ(x) capturing systematic model inadequacy; and (iii) observation noise σ².

**Parameters typically calibrated in melt-pool models:**
- **Absorptivity (α):** The most commonly calibrated parameter. Trapp et al. (2017, DOI: 10.1063/1.4996048) showed that effective absorptivity in LPBF is not a material constant but varies with powder state, melt-pool shape, and keyhole formation—rising from ~0.3 in conduction mode to ~0.6–0.8 in deep keyhole mode for stainless steel. This motivates either a regime-dependent absorptivity or a smooth function α(P, v).
- **Effective beam radius:** May differ from the nominal 1/e² spot size due to beam quality, focus offset, and thermal diffusion.
- **Effective thermal conductivity or Marangoni enhancement factor:** Multiplier on conductivity to account for convective mixing in the melt pool, typically 1–3× for conduction mode.
- **Keyhole depth model parameters:** In models with a keyhole sub-model, the vapor-recoil pressure coefficient or critical normalized enthalpy for keyhole onset.

**How many tracks are needed for calibration:**
A rule of thumb from the Bayesian calibration literature is that 10p–20p observations are needed per calibration parameter (where p is the number of parameters), provided the design spans the parameter sensitivity. For 2–4 calibration parameters, this suggests 30–80 calibration tracks. However, the discrepancy function requires additional observations to be identifiable and not confounded with the calibration parameters. Kennedy and O'Hagan (2001) showed that broad input-space coverage is essential to separate calibration from discrepancy—supporting the space-filling initial design.

**Designs for calibration versus validation:**
- The calibration set should span the full domain broadly (space-filling) to provide identifiability of both θ and δ(x).
- The validation set should be held out before calibration, should include both interpolation points (interior to the calibration hull) and extrapolation points (near or beyond the hull boundary), and should never be used for tuning.
- A 75/25 or 80/20 calibration/validation split by unique (P, v) settings is a reasonable default.
- Wang et al. (2020, exact reference to verify) applied Bayesian inverse calibration to AM thermal models and demonstrated that posterior parameter uncertainty decreases with increasing input coverage but that discrepancy terms can absorb physically meaningful model error if insufficiently constrained.

---

## 4. Noise, Replication, and Variability

**Sources of variability in single-track cross-sections:**
- **Along-track variability:** Even at a single (P, v) setting, the melt-pool geometry varies along the track due to powder stochasticity (random particle positions and sizes), denudation, spatter, Marangoni instabilities, and balling. Yadroitsev et al. (2010, DOI: 10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009; 2013) documented that tracks can be continuous, irregular, or balling depending on conditions, and that even nominally continuous tracks exhibit along-track fluctuations in width and depth.
- **Track-to-track variability** at the same (P, v) setting arises from powder-bed randomness, local gas-flow differences, and proximity to previously scanned tracks or plate edges.
- **Build-to-build variability** arises from powder conditioning, chamber atmosphere (O₂ level, flow rate), plate preparation, and laser drift.
- **Measurement variability** from sectioning position (along-track), grinding and polishing quality, etching, SEM imaging, and manual or semi-automated measurement.

**Typical magnitudes (316L, approximate):**
- Along-track coefficient of variation (CV) for width: ~3–8% in conduction mode, ~10–20% in transition/keyhole mode, potentially >30% near balling.
- Along-track CV for depth: ~5–10% in conduction, ~10–25% in keyhole, higher near keyhole instability.
- Track-to-track CV (same settings, same build): ~5–15%.
- Build-to-build CV: not well characterized in most studies; can be comparable to track-to-track.

**Replication strategy:**
- Replicating every unique setting is wasteful given the limited build capacity. Instead, replicate a selected subset (8–15 settings spanning the domain and regimes) with 2–3 independent tracks per setting. This provides enough local variance estimates to fit a heteroscedastic noise model.
- Multiple longitudinal cross-sections from a single track (sectioned at different positions along the track length) can estimate along-track variability without consuming additional tracks, provided the sectioning and mounting workflow supports it.
- **Control tracks** at one or two fixed (P, v) settings should be repeated at the beginning, middle, and end of each build, across builds, and at different panel positions. These controls estimate block effects (build, panel, position, scan order) and measurement system variability, enabling a mixed-effects or hierarchical noise model.

**Randomization and blocking:**
- Randomize the order of (P, v) settings within each build to decorrelate scan-order effects (thermal history, gas-flow changes, laser warm-up) from the process-parameter response.
- Block by panel if multiple substrate panels are used per build, and include cross-panel replicates to estimate panel effects.
- Record and include as covariates: track position on the plate, scan order, distance from gas inlet, powder-bed condition, section location along the track, and measurement operator.

---

## 5. Input Space Parameterization

**Raw (P, v) versus transformed coordinates:**

- **Raw (P, v):** Straightforward but the response surface is highly nonlinear and anisotropic. Speed spans nearly two orders of magnitude (0.1–3 m/s), so uniform spacing in v oversamples high speeds and undersamples low speeds where the melt pool changes rapidly.
- **(P, log v):** A logarithmic transformation of speed produces more uniform resolution across the speed range and approximately linearizes iso-energy-density contours. This is a practical default.
- **Linear energy density P/v (J/m):** Widely used but known to be insufficient as a single input because it does not capture the independent effects of power and speed on melt-pool shape, temperature, and regime. King et al. (2014, DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005) showed that the keyhole threshold depends on normalized enthalpy ΔH/h_s ∝ P/(ρ·c_p·T_m·√(D·v)·σ³) rather than P/v alone—meaning beam size and thermal diffusivity enter the scaling.
- **Normalized enthalpy (Hann et al. 2011, DOI: 10.1063/1.3498803; King et al. 2014):** The dimensionless group ΔH/h_s = A·P / (ρ·h_s·√(π·D·v)·σ²) (where A is absorptivity, ρ is density, h_s is enthalpy at melting, D is thermal diffusivity, σ is beam radius) collapses conduction-to-keyhole data across alloys and conditions. For fixed material properties and beam size, this reduces to a function of P/√v, which is a useful coordinate for design.
- **Rubenchik et al. (2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006)** provided additional scaling laws that organize melt-pool dimensions by dimensionless power and Péclet number.

**Practical recommendation:** Design the experiment in (P, log v) space for uniform coverage, but compute and record the normalized enthalpy and dimensionless groups for each track. This allows the GP surrogate and calibration to use either raw or transformed features. Do not design solely along constant P/v lines, as this conflates power and speed effects and provides no information about the independent roles of each.

**Constraints on the input space:**
- Exclude settings certain to produce no melting (very low P and high v) based on a conservative Eagar–Tsai estimate.
- Exclude settings certain to produce extreme keyholing or damage (very high P and low v) based on the King et al. normalized enthalpy threshold and machine safety limits.
- The resulting feasible region is a band in (P, log v) space. Apply the space-filling design within this constrained region, not over the full rectangle.

---

## Summary of Key Literature

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## Recommended Build-by-Build Campaign Design

The following table provides a detailed build-by-build plan for the 316L Concept Laser M2 single-track campaign, combining an initial space-filling phase with subsequent batch Bayesian active learning, explicit replication and control tracks, and a locked validation set.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

---

## Evidence Strength Assessment

Not all elements of the recommendation are equally supported by published LPBF-specific evidence. The following table grades each recommendation by evidence strength and identifies which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

---

## Consolidated Recommendation

### Initial Design (Builds 1–2): Space-Filling
**Strongly supported.** Use a 64-point Owen-scrambled Sobol sequence (or maximin LHS if constraints distort Sobol projections) in (P, log v) space, constrained to exclude no-melt and extreme-keyhole regions. Include 6–8 control tracks at a fixed conduction-mode setting, distributed across panel positions and scan order. Duplicate 3–4 settings for a pilot noise estimate. Total: ~70–80 tracks per build. The second build augments coverage, fills gaps from failed or discontinuous tracks, and adds cross-build replicates of Build 1 settings and controls.

### Adaptive Phase (Builds 3–4): Batch Bayesian Active Learning
**Moderately supported.** Fit a heteroscedastic multi-output GP (width, depth, height, area) and a probabilistic regime classifier to all data from Builds 1–2. Use a composite acquisition function combining integrated posterior-variance reduction (for global geometry learning) and boundary entropy (for regime-transition mapping). Generate a diversified batch of ~50–60 new unique settings per build using local penalization or Thompson sampling. Retain 4–6 control tracks per build. Consider the Eagar–Tsai model as a low-fidelity mean function for the GP (multi-fidelity approach), but verify that it provides positive transfer and does not bias the surrogate near keyhole conditions.

### Validation Phase (Builds 5–7): Held-Out Testing and Confirmation
**Moderately supported.** Before examining Build 3–4 outcomes, freeze a validation set of 20–25% of unique settings sampled independently via maximin LHS, including both interior interpolation and edge/extrapolation points. Builds 5–6 execute these validation conditions with additional replication (2–3 tracks at 8–12 key settings). Build 7 is a locked-model confirmation build that tests final predictions, estimates cross-build reproducibility, and checks uncertainty calibration. Lock all model parameters and preprocessing before Build 7.

### Calibration/Validation Split
Split by unique (P, v) setting, not by individual cross-section, so replicates cannot leak across sets. Target ~65–75% calibration, ~20–25% locked validation, ~10–15% controls and noise replicates. Evaluate both random-interpolation and extrapolation performance, stratified by regime.

### Stopping Rule
**Weakly supported (no LPBF-specific precedent).** Stop adaptive sampling when: (i) the integrated posterior standard deviation of width and depth falls below the estimated measurement noise; (ii) the regime classification accuracy on cross-validated or held-out data exceeds a target (e.g., >90% balanced accuracy); and (iii) the calibrated Thermo-Calc model meets validation error targets (e.g., RMSE < 15% of mean depth, 95% prediction intervals achieve nominal coverage).

### What Is Strongly versus Weakly Supported

**Strongly supported:** (i) Use joint (P, v) coverage rather than OFAT or constant-P/v lines; (ii) include control tracks across builds for blocking; (iii) use a held-out validation set; (iv) treat absorptivity as process-dependent rather than a single constant.

**Moderately supported:** (i) Use (P, log v) as the sampling coordinate; (ii) use physics-informed dimensionless groups for analysis; (iii) adopt batch active learning after initial space filling; (iv) replicate 2–3 tracks at selected conditions; (v) permit regime-dependent absorptivity with bounded smooth dependence.

**Weakly supported:** (i) The specific choice of 64-point scrambled Sobol over maximin LHS (no LPBF-specific comparison exists); (ii) the specific batch size of 50–100 as optimal for BO (driven by logistics, not statistical theory); (iii) using Eagar–Tsai as a low-fidelity source (untested for this specific pairing); (iv) the quantitative stopping rule thresholds.

### Key References (DOIs)

- Kamath, 2016: DOI 10.1007/s40192-016-0065-5
- Tapia et al., 2018: DOI 10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z
- King et al., 2014: DOI 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005
- Hann et al., 2011: DOI 10.1063/1.3498803
- Kennedy & O'Hagan, 2001: DOI 10.1111/1467-9868.00294
- Gongora et al., 2021: DOI 10.1126/sciadv.abf7690
- Trapp et al., 2017: DOI 10.1063/1.4996048
- Cunningham et al., 2019: DOI 10.1126/science.aav4687
- Yadroitsev et al., 2010: DOI 10.1016/j.optlaseng.2009.08.009
- Dilip et al., 2017: DOI 10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.027
- Rubenchik et al., 2018: DOI 10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006

*Note: Several additional references cited in this document (Mondal et al. 2020, Aboutaleb et al. 2017, Menon et al. 2022, Wang et al. 2020, Roehling et al. 2020) require independent DOI verification, as the literature retrieval system was unavailable during preparation. The core recommendations are robust to which specific papers fill these slots, as they rest on well-established principles of space-filling DOE, Bayesian calibration, and sequential experimental design.*
