### Replication strategy

- **Do not replicate every setting.** With 50–100 tracks per build and 250–600 total, replicating all settings halves the unique coverage.
- **Replicate a selected subset** of 8–15 settings spanning low, medium, and high energy densities and all regimes, with 2–3 independent tracks each. This provides local variance estimates for a heteroscedastic noise model.
- **Multiple longitudinal sections** from a single track can estimate along-track variability without consuming additional scan vectors.
- **Control tracks:** Repeat 1–2 fixed (P, v) settings at the beginning, middle, and end of each build, across all builds, and at different panel positions. These estimate build effects, position effects, and measurement-system variability.

### Randomization and blocking

- **Randomize** the order of (P, v) settings within each build to decorrelate scan-order effects from process-parameter response.
- **Block** by panel if multiple panels per build; include cross-panel replicates.
- **Record covariates:** track position, scan order, distance from gas inlet, powder condition, section location along track, measurement operator.

---

## 5. Input Space Parameterization

### Coordinate systems

| Coordinate | Advantages | Limitations |
|---|---|---|
| Raw (P, v) | Machine-interpretable; no transformation needed | Response surface is nonlinear and anisotropic; v spans ~2 decades |
| (P, log v) | More uniform resolution across 0.1–3 m/s; approximately linearizes iso-energy contours | Minor: log transform complicates batch-BO boundary constraints |

| Normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs | Collapses conduction–keyhole transition across alloys; physically motivated | Requires assumed absorptivity (which is being calibrated); for fixed material and beam, reduces to P/√v |
| Dimensionless power + Péclet number | Full physics-informed scaling (Hann et al. 2011, Rubenchik et al. 2018) | More complex; scaling may break across powder/substrate transitions and keyhole regime |

King et al. (2014; DOI: 10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005) showed that keyholing depends on normalized enthalpy ΔH/hs ∝ A·P / (ρ·hs·√(π·D·v)·σ²) rather than P/v alone, meaning beam size and thermal diffusivity enter the scaling. (2018; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2018.06.006) provided additional scaling laws.

**Strongly supported.** Generate a 64-point Owen-scrambled Sobol sequence in normalized (P, log v) space, constrained to the feasible region between conservative no-melt and excessive-keyhole bounds. The 64-point Sobol is chosen because it is a power of two (preserving digital-net balance) and fits within the build capacity while leaving room for controls. Most published LPBF single-track studies have used **structured factorial grids** or **one-factor-at-a-time sweeps**. Dilip et al. (2017; DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2017.10.027) used dense power–speed grids to classify single-track regimes. Yadroitsev et al. No LPBF study has published a head-to-head comparison of scrambled Sobol, maximin LHS, or Halton sequences against a grid at equal sample size. However, Tapia et al. (2018; DOI: 10.1007/s00170-017-1045-z) fitted GP surrogates to 316L melt-pool geometry, and the GP formulation implicitly benefits from space-filling coverage. The computer-experiment DOE literature (Santner, Williams, and Notz, Springer, 2003) consistently shows that quasi-random space-filling designs provide lower integrated prediction variance per point than grids in 2–4D.

**What space-filling designs offer:** (i) more uniform coverage per track; (ii) better support for GP/polynomial surrogates without aliasing; (iii) compatibility with sequential augmentation (Sobol doubles; LHS augments by optimization).

For a laser powder bed fusion single-track campaign whose goal is to calibrate and validate a melt-pool model (the Thermo-Calc AM Module, steady state) against measured cross-sections, how should the power-speed (and possibly spot-size or layer) settings be chosen: a quasi-random space-filling design such as scrambled Sobol or Latin hypercube, or batch Bayesian optimization / active learning, and with what batch sizes and replicates? Context: we are planning single-track laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) experiments in 316L stainless steel on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (continuous-wave Yb fibre laser at about 1070 nm, 200 W or 400 W depending on configuration, focused spot about 50-90 um 1/e^2 diameter, galvanometer scanner, nitrogen or argon shielding gas flowing across the plate). Commercial gas-atomized 316L powder (about 15-45 um) is spread as ONE powder layer (nominally 30-50 um) on 316L substrate panels (roughly 80 mm square, bolted flush into a 250 mm build plate), and each track is a single scan vector with its own laser power P and scan speed v (P about 50-400 W, v about 0.1-3 m/s). Each build holds tens to about a hundred tracks. After the build we cut the panels with a bandsaw and a precision abrasive saw, grind to a section plane perpendicular to the scan direction (a transverse cross-section through all tracks in a row at once), mount, polish, etch and image in an SEM, and measure melt-pool width, depth below the substrate surface, height above it and area, and classify the regime (lack of fusion/discontinuous, balling, conduction, transition, keyhole). The measured cross-sections will be compared with STEADY-STATE single-track predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-derived properties, Gaussian or keyhole heat source with absorptivity to calibrate), and with the analytical Eagar-Tsai model (travelling Gaussian surface source, constant properties). We want to calibrate the model's heat-source parameters on part of the tracks and validate on the rest. We expect roughly 50-100 tracks per build, about one build per week, 4-7 builds in total (about 250-600 tracks), with sectioning and SEM as the bottleneck.

Please answer each part with citations and DOIs:
1. Published uses of space-filling designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton) versus grids or one-factor-at-a-time sweeps for LPBF single tracks or process windows, and what they gained.
2. Published uses of Bayesian optimization, active learning or sequential design for LPBF single tracks, printability maps and melt-pool regimes (e.g. keyhole and lack-of-fusion boundaries, balling): the objectives and acquisition functions (expected improvement, uncertainty sampling, integrated variance reduction, level-set or boundary estimation, classification-based), the surrogate (Gaussian process, multi-fidelity with an analytical or FE model as low fidelity), batch sizes, and how many tracks they needed. Examples might include Tapia et al. 2018 (GP for 316L melt-pool depth on single tracks), Kamath 2016, Mondal et al. 2020, Sheikh/Arroyave group printability and BO work, Menon et al., Gongora/Brown (BEAR), Aboutaleb et al., Wang et al.
3. Bayesian model calibration (Kennedy-O'Hagan style, with a discrepancy term) of melt-pool models to single-track data: which parameters were calibrated (absorptivity, its dependence on energy density or keyhole depth, beam radius, effective conductivity, Marangoni enhancement), how many tracks were needed, and which designs worked best for calibration versus validation (held-out points, extrapolation tests).
4. Noise and replication: the run-to-run, track-to-track and along-track variability of measured width and depth in 316L single tracks; how many replicates or cross-sections per setting are needed; using repeated control tracks to estimate noise and block effects (build, panel, position on the plate); randomization and blocking.
5. Which input space to sample: raw (P, v), (P, log v), linear energy P/v, normalized enthalpy or the dimensionless groups of King et al. 2014 / Hann et al., and the effect of constraints such as excluding settings certain to not melt or to keyhole badly.

Finish with a recommendation for our case: the initial design (method, number of points, whether to use a power of two for Sobol, controls and replicates per build), the batch BO/active-learning formulation for later builds (objective, acquisition, batch size equal to one build, stopping rule), and the split between calibration and held-out validation tracks. Flag which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.

Question: For a laser powder bed fusion single-track campaign whose goal is to calibrate and validate a melt-pool model (the Thermo-Calc AM Module, steady state) against measured cross-sections, how should the power-speed (and possibly spot-size or layer) settings be chosen: a quasi-random space-filling design such as scrambled Sobol or Latin hypercube, or batch Bayesian optimization / active learning, and with what batch sizes and replicates? Context: we are planning single-track laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) experiments in 316L stainless steel on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (continuous-wave Yb fibre laser at about 1070 nm, 200 W or 400 W depending on configuration, focused spot about 50-90 um 1/e^2 diameter, galvanometer scanner, nitrogen or argon shielding gas flowing across the plate). Commercial gas-atomized 316L powder (about 15-45 um) is spread as ONE powder layer (nominally 30-50 um) on 316L substrate panels (roughly 80 mm square, bolted flush into a 250 mm build plate), and each track is a single scan vector with its own laser power P and scan speed v (P about 50-400 W, v about 0.1-3 m/s). Each build holds tens to about a hundred tracks. After the build we cut the panels with a bandsaw and a precision abrasive saw, grind to a section plane perpendicular to the scan direction (a transverse cross-section through all tracks in a row at once), mount, polish, etch and image in an SEM, and measure melt-pool width, depth below the substrate surface, height above it and area, and classify the regime (lack of fusion/discontinuous, balling, conduction, transition, keyhole). The measured cross-sections will be compared with STEADY-STATE single-track predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-derived properties, Gaussian or keyhole heat source with absorptivity to calibrate), and with the analytical Eagar-Tsai model (travelling Gaussian surface source, constant properties). We want to calibrate the model's heat-source parameters on part of the tracks and validate on the rest. We expect roughly 50-100 tracks per build, about one build per week, 4-7 builds in total (about 250-600 tracks), with sectioning and SEM as the bottleneck.

Please answer each part with citations and DOIs:
1. Published uses of space-filling designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton) versus grids or one-factor-at-a-time sweeps for LPBF single tracks or process windows, and what they gained.
2. Published uses of Bayesian optimization, active learning or sequential design for LPBF single tracks, printability maps and melt-pool regimes (e.g. keyhole and lack-of-fusion boundaries, balling): the objectives and acquisition functions (expected improvement, uncertainty sampling, integrated variance reduction, level-set or boundary estimation, classification-based), the surrogate (Gaussian process, multi-fidelity with an analytical or FE model as low fidelity), batch sizes, and how many tracks they needed. Examples might include Tapia et al. 2018 (GP for 316L melt-pool depth on single tracks), Kamath 2016, Mondal et al. 2020, Sheikh/Arroyave group printability and BO work, Menon et al., Gongora/Brown (BEAR), Aboutaleb et al., Wang et al.
3. Bayesian model calibration (Kennedy-O'Hagan style, with a discrepancy term) of melt-pool models to single-track data: which parameters were calibrated (absorptivity, its dependence on energy density or keyhole depth, beam radius, effective conductivity, Marangoni enhancement), how many tracks were needed, and which designs worked best for calibration versus validation (held-out points, extrapolation tests).
4. Noise and replication: the run-to-run, track-to-track and along-track variability of measured width and depth in 316L single tracks; how many replicates or cross-sections per setting are needed; using repeated control tracks to estimate noise and block effects (build, panel, position on the plate); randomization and blocking.
5. Which input space to sample: raw (P, v), (P, log v), linear energy P/v, normalized enthalpy or the dimensionless groups of King et al. 2014 / Hann et al., and the effect of constraints such as excluding settings certain to not melt or to keyhole badly.

Finish with a recommendation for our case: the initial design (method, number of points, whether to use a power of two for Sobol, controls and replicates per build), the batch BO/active-learning formulation for later builds (objective, acquisition, batch size equal to one build, stopping rule), and the split between calibration and held-out validation tracks. Flag which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.

info.query:
For a laser powder bed fusion single-track campaign whose goal is to calibrate and validate a melt-pool model (the Thermo-Calc AM Module, steady state) against measured cross-sections, how should the power-speed (and possibly spot-size or layer) settings be chosen: a quasi-random space-filling design such as scrambled Sobol or Latin hypercube, or batch Bayesian optimization / active learning, and with what batch sizes and replicates? Context: we are planning single-track laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) experiments in 316L stainless steel on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (continuous-wave Yb fibre laser at about 1070 nm, 200 W or 400 W depending on configuration, focused spot about 50-90 um 1/e^2 diameter, galvanometer scanner, nitrogen or argon shielding gas flowing across the plate). Commercial gas-atomized 316L powder (about 15-45 um) is spread as ONE powder layer (nominally 30-50 um) on 316L substrate panels (roughly 80 mm square, bolted flush into a 250 mm build plate), and each track is a single scan vector with its own laser power P and scan speed v (P about 50-400 W, v about 0.1-3 m/s). Each build holds tens to about a hundred tracks. After the build we cut the panels with a bandsaw and a precision abrasive saw, grind to a section plane perpendicular to the scan direction (a transverse cross-section through all tracks in a row at once), mount, polish, etch and image in an SEM, and measure melt-pool width, depth below the substrate surface, height above it and area, and classify the regime (lack of fusion/discontinuous, balling, conduction, transition, keyhole). The measured cross-sections will be compared with STEADY-STATE single-track predictions of the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-derived properties, Gaussian or keyhole heat source with absorptivity to calibrate), and with the analytical Eagar-Tsai model (travelling Gaussian surface source, constant properties). We want to calibrate the model's heat-source parameters on part of the tracks and validate on the rest. We expect roughly 50-100 tracks per build, about one build per week, 4-7 builds in total (about 250-600 tracks), with sectioning and SEM as the bottleneck.

Please answer each part with citations and DOIs:
1. Published uses of space-filling designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton) versus grids or one-factor-at-a-time sweeps for LPBF single tracks or process windows, and what they gained.
2. Published uses of Bayesian optimization, active learning or sequential design for LPBF single tracks, printability maps and melt-pool regimes (e.g. keyhole and lack-of-fusion boundaries, balling): the objectives and acquisition functions (expected improvement, uncertainty sampling, integrated variance reduction, level-set or boundary estimation, classification-based), the surrogate (Gaussian process, multi-fidelity with an analytical or FE model as low fidelity), batch sizes, and how many tracks they needed. Examples might include Tapia et al. 2018 (GP for 316L melt-pool depth on single tracks), Kamath 2016, Mondal et al. 2020, Sheikh/Arroyave group printability and BO work, Menon et al., Gongora/Brown (BEAR), Aboutaleb et al., Wang et al.
3. Bayesian model calibration (Kennedy-O'Hagan style, with a discrepancy term) of melt-pool models to single-track data: which parameters were calibrated (absorptivity, its dependence on energy density or keyhole depth, beam radius, effective conductivity, Marangoni enhancement), how many tracks were needed, and which designs worked best for calibration versus validation (held-out points, extrapolation tests).
4. Noise and replication: the run-to-run, track-to-track and along-track variability of measured width and depth in 316L single tracks; how many replicates or cross-sections per setting are needed; using repeated control tracks to estimate noise and block effects (build, panel, position on the plate); randomization and blocking.
5. Which input space to sample: raw (P, v), (P, log v), linear energy P/v, normalized enthalpy or the dimensionless groups of King et al. 2014 / Hann et al., and the effect of constraints such as excluding settings certain to not melt or to keyhole badly.

Finish with a recommendation for our case: the initial design (method, number of points, whether to use a power of two for Sobol, controls and replicates per build), the batch BO/active-learning formulation for later builds (objective, acquisition, batch size equal to one build, stopping rule), and the split between calibration and held-out validation tracks. Flag which choices are strongly versus weakly supported.
